angle: How did a print that cost about two bowls of noodles become a $2.76 million icon, made by a man who thought he had barely started?
hooks: The most famous wave in art was printed up to eight thousand times.
The man who made this said nothing he drew before seventy was worth noticing.

painting.title: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
painting.museum: Impressions in the Met, the British Museum and others

script.text: Brand new, this print cost a little more than two bowls of noodles.
Hokusai made it around 1831, aged about seventy, for a series of views of Mount Fuji.
script.say: Hokusai made it around eighteen thirty-one, aged about seventy, for a series of views of Mount Fuji.

script.text: But where is Fuji? Look below the claws of foam: that small triangle is Japan's tallest mountain.
Those boats are express barges racing fresh fish to Edo, and the wave towers about ten metres over them.
Its selling point was a new imported pigment, Prussian blue.
Printers pressed it twice where the wave is deepest, to give the water depth and movement.
It was never meant to be rare: up to eight thousand copies were printed, until the woodblocks wore out.
In 2023, one early copy sold for 2.76 million dollars.
script.say: In twenty twenty-three, one early copy sold for two point seven six million dollars.

script.text: Yet Hokusai thought he had barely started.
A few years later he wrote that nothing he drew before seventy was worth noticing.
At a hundred and ten, he promised, every dot and every line would be alive.
He died at eighty-nine, asking heaven for five more years to become a real artist.

post.caption:
It once cost about two bowls of noodles. One copy just sold for $2.76 million. And the man who made it thought he'd barely started.
Which detail did you never notice before?
